screens.title: Implementing Gaze and Pointer Interactions
screens.subtitle: How to let users select objects by looking or pointing in XR using the XR Interaction Toolkit

narration.text: In this lesson you'll learn two core interaction families for XR: gaze-based selection and pointer-based selection. Gaze interaction lets a user select by looking at an object long enough for a dwell to complete. Pointer interaction uses a virtual ray from a controller or hand to target distant objects, with a visible line and a reticle at the hit point. Both approaches are common in VR and AR and are essential for menus, object selection, and interactions when your hands can't directly reach a surface. You'll see the concrete Unity components used: the XR Gaze Interactor for camera-based gaze, XRSimpleInteractable on targets, and the XR Ray Interactor paired with an XR Interactor Line Visual for controller pointers. We'll also show small C# scripts that subscribe to hover and select events so you can change materials, log selection, or trigger game behavior. Finally, we'll highlight common setup mistakes — layer masks, colliders, and rigidbody settings — and how to test them quickly. By the end you'll be able to create a gaze-activated button and a ray-selectable cube, tune feedback so users know what they are pointing at, and debug why a ray might pass through an object.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Use XR Gaze Interactor for camera-based dwell selection and XR Ray Interactor plus Line Visual for controller-based ray selection. Combine XRSimpleInteractable events with lightweight C# handlers and clear visual feedback.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter — practical, testable skills

narration.text: In this set of objectives we move from understanding to doing. First, you will implement gaze-based selection so objects can be chosen simply by sustained attention. Practically, this means adding an XRSimpleInteractable to a GameObject and enabling a gaze dwell so the system fires a select event after a short delay. Second, you will configure an XR Ray Interactor so handheld controllers can point at distant objects. That includes attaching an XR Interactor Line Visual and setting the Interaction Layer Mask to include your interactable object layers. Third, you will write C# scripts that subscribe to the simple interactable events — hover enter, hover exit, and select — to trigger color changes, logs, or gameplay actions. Subscribing and removing listeners correctly prevents memory leaks and keeps behavior predictable. Fourth, you will learn to identify common raycast and collision problems, such as wrong layers, trigger colliders without appropriate rigidbodies, or colliders scaled too small, and how to test these quickly in Play Mode. Each objective maps to a concrete lab step so you can prove competency by building two cubes and scripting their hover and select behavior.

screens.title: Gaze Interaction: Definition and Use Cases
screens.subtitle: What gaze interaction is, when to use it, and common pitfalls

narration.text: Gaze interaction is an input method where the user looks at an object and, after a specified dwell time, triggers a selection or activation. This is powerful when hands are unavailable, when you want a low-friction UI in VR, or when AR overlays require quick attention-based choices. In Unity, gaze-based selection is usually provided by an XR Gaze Interactor attached to the Main Camera. That interactor casts a ray forward from the user’s head and reports hover events when the ray intersects an XRSimpleInteractable. A practical example is a menu where looking at a button for two seconds opens a panel. The simple mechanics are: the camera gaze ray hits an interactable, the XRSimpleInteractable fires firstHoverEntered, a dwell timer completes, then selectEntered fires. A common misconception is thinking gaze is “always more precise” than pointing. In practice gaze can be noisy: head jitter, inaccurate tracking, and small target sizes make dwell frustrating. Use clear visual feedback — color change, outlines, or a radial progress indicator — to show progress toward selection. Also tune dwell time; two seconds is a common starting point but may need adjustment for your audience. Finally, test accessibility: people with limited head control may need controller-based alternatives. Reflect: when does your app benefit more from gaze versus pointer selection?

keyIdea.title: Gaze definition
keyIdea.text: Gaze selects by sustained looking and is implemented with XR Gaze Interactor and XRSimpleInteractable; always pair it with clear progress feedback.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Gaze Interaction: Definition and Use Cases
What is Gaze Interaction?
A camera-originated ray detects look-based hover and, after a dwell timer, triggers selection. It is ideal for hands-free or head-tracked flows.
When to use: menus, selection at distance, quick look-based choices in VR and AR.
Misconception: Gaze is not always more precise — head jitter and small targets reduce reliability.
Good practice: add a progress indicator for dwell and tune dwell time for comfort.
Key Takeaway

Gaze works when hands aren’t available, but only if you give clear progress feedback and tune dwell time for your users.

Concrete Example
A gaze-activated button: add XRSimpleInteractable to a cube, set Gaze Dwell Time to 2 seconds, then subscribe to selectEntered to open a panel or play a sound.
Visual cues to add
  • Change material on firstHoverEntered.
  • Show a radial progress indicator during dwell.
  • Reset visuals on lastHoverExited.
Check your understanding: When might gaze cause user frustration, and what visual design reduces that frustration?

screens.title: GazeInteractableColorChange — Script Walkthrough
screens.subtitle: How to subscribe to hover and select events to change materials safely

narration.text: Let's walk through a compact C# script that responds to gaze hover and selection events on an XRSimpleInteractable. The script's purpose is straightforward: when the user's gaze hovers over the object, swap the material to a hover material; when gaze exits, restore the default material; when dwell completes and selectEntered fires, run the selection action. Key implementation details are: get the MeshRenderer and XRSimpleInteractable in Awake, subscribe to firstHoverEntered, lastHoverExited, and selectEntered, and always remove listeners in OnDestroy to avoid dangling subscriptions. A common mistake is assuming selectEntered will fire without configuring the interactable's Gaze Dwell Time — if that value is zero, dwell selects won't happen automatically. The example code here is the exact pattern to use. After you attach this script to a cube and assign the hover and default materials in the Inspector, test in Play Mode by looking at the cube for the dwell duration. Watch Debug. Log output to confirm events fired. Misconception alert: swapping the renderer's shared material affects all instances that reference it; use instance materials if you want per-object changes. Now we'll show the code you can drop into a component and test.

keyIdea.title: Event-driven pattern
keyIdea.text: Subscribe to hover and select events in Awake and remove them in OnDestroy; ensure Gaze Dwell Time is set for selectEntered to fire.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › GazeInteractableColorChange — Script Walkthrough
Readable Code Panel
Copy this script into a C# file named GazeInteractableColorChange and attach it to your cube with an XRSimpleInteractable.
using UnityEngine;
using UnityEngine.XR.Interaction.Toolkit;

public class GazeInteractableColorChange : MonoBehaviour
{
    [SerializeField] private Material hoverMaterial;
    [SerializeField] private Material defaultMaterial;
    private MeshRenderer meshRenderer;
    private XRSimpleInteractable interactable;

    void Awake()
    {
        meshRenderer = GetComponent<MeshRenderer>();
        interactable = GetComponent<XRSimpleInteractable>();

        if (interactable != null)
        {
            interactable.firstHoverEntered.AddListener(OnGazeEnter);
            interactable.lastHoverExited.AddListener(OnGazeExit);
            interactable.selectEntered.AddListener(OnGazeSelect); // For dwell-based selection
        }
    }

    private void OnDestroy()
    {
        if (interactable != null)
        {
            interactable.firstHoverEntered.RemoveListener(OnGazeEnter);
            interactable.lastHoverExited.RemoveListener(OnGazeExit);
            interactable.selectEntered.RemoveListener(OnGazeSelect);
        }
    }

    private void OnGazeEnter(HoverEnterEventArgs args)
    {
        if (meshRenderer != null && hoverMaterial != null)
        {
            meshRenderer.material = hoverMaterial;
            Debug.Log("Gaze entered: " + gameObject.name);
        }
    }

    private void OnGazeExit(HoverExitEventArgs args)
    {
        if (meshRenderer != null && defaultMaterial != null)
        {
            meshRenderer.material = defaultMaterial;
            Debug.Log("Gaze exited: " + gameObject.name);
        }
    }

    private void OnGazeSelect(SelectEnterEventArgs args)
    {
        Debug.Log("Gaze selected: " + gameObject.name);
        // Trigger specific action after dwell time
    }
}
Notes and Gotchas
  • Set the XRSimpleInteractable's Gaze Dwell Time > 0 for selectEntered to fire automatically.
  • Use instance materials if you don't want shared-material side effects when swapping materials.
  • Remove listeners in OnDestroy to avoid memory leaks and unexpected callbacks.
Common Mistake

Leaving Gaze Dwell Time at zero prevents selectEntered; hover events still fire but selection won't occur automatically.

Try this: set Gaze Dwell Time to 2 seconds, look at the cube, and watch the Debug.Log lines to confirm OnGazeEnter, OnGazeExit, and OnGazeSelect firing.

screens.title: Pointer (Ray) Interaction: How It Works
screens.subtitle: Understanding XR Ray Interactor, line visuals, and reticles for controller targeting

narration.text: Pointer interaction uses a ray projected from a controller or hand to target objects at a distance. In Unity's XR Interaction Toolkit this is implemented with an XR Ray Interactor component placed on a controller GameObject, typically under your XR Origin's Left and Right hand controllers. When paired with an XR Interactor Line Visual, the ray is visible as a laser with an optional reticle at the hit point so users can judge distance and where a selection will occur. When the ray intersects an XRSimpleInteractable, the interactor can call hover events and, on input such as a trigger press, fire select events. Key practical items: set the Interaction Layer Mask on the XR Ray Interactor so it only targets layers you intend. If an object is on a layer not included the ray will pass through it. Also ensure your target object has a proper Collider; trigger colliders sometimes need an accompanying Rigidbody to be detected reliably in some physics configurations. A common misconception is that the line visual alone guarantees interaction; it only shows what the ray is doing — the interactor's masks and the object's collider configuration determine whether the ray registers a hit. Test with simple cubes and check the reticle moves and hover events are logged before attempting complex scenes. How could you verify the problem if the ray misses? Start by checking layers and colliders.

keyIdea.title: Pointer essentials
keyIdea.text: XR Ray Interactor produces the ray; XR Interactor Line Visual provides the visible laser and reticle; Interaction Layer Mask and colliders determine hit results.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Pointer (Ray) Interaction: How It Works
XR Ray Interactor Basics
Attach XR Ray Interactor to controller objects. Pair with XR Interactor Line Visual to draw the pointer and reticle.
Interaction Layer Mask: include only layers that should be targeted.
Collider requirements: non-trigger colliders detect hits reliably; triggers may need Rigidbody adjustments.
Reticle: gives precise hit feedback and helps gauge distance.
Concrete Example
Add XR Ray Interactor to LeftHand Controller and RightHand Controller. Add XR Interactor Line Visual to the same GameObjects. Confirm the reticle appears when the ray hits a cube with an XRSimpleInteractable.
Check your understanding: If the ray misses an object that has an XRSimpleInteractable, what are the first two properties to verify? (Hint: layer mask and collider configuration.)
Common Mistake

Leaving interaction layers unconfigured or having trigger colliders with no Rigidbody can make the ray pass through objects.

screens.title: RaySelectableColorChange — Script Walkthrough
screens.subtitle: Change color on hover and log selection on trigger press for ray pointers

narration.text: This script follows the same event-driven pattern as the gaze example but is tuned for pointer interactions. The XRSimpleInteractable fires firstHoverEntered and lastHoverExited when a ray intersects and leaves the object, and selectEntered when a controller input (for example, pressing the trigger) causes selection. The script obtains MeshRenderer and XRSimpleInteractable in Awake and subscribes to the three events. In OnRayHoverEnter you swap to the hover material and log the interaction. In OnRayHoverExit you restore the default material. In OnRaySelect you log which interactor selected the object by reading the interactorObject transform name from the SelectEnterEventArgs. This helps when both hands can select the same object, so you can differentiate left from right. A practical tip: if you plan to move objects with physics after selection, ensure the object has a Rigidbody configured appropriately. If you only need a visual response, a MeshRenderer swap is sufficient and low-cost. Test by pointing your controller ray, watch the hover color change, then press trigger and verify the select log entry that includes the selecting interactor's name. That confirms both hover and select flows work.

keyIdea.title: Pointer script pattern
keyIdea.text: Use firstHoverEntered and lastHoverExited to show hover, and selectEntered to act on trigger-based selection; log interactor identity to distinguish sources.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › RaySelectableColorChange — Script Walkthrough
Code to paste into RaySelectableColorChange.cs
This script listens to hover and select events for pointer-based interactions.
using UnityEngine;
using UnityEngine.XR.Interaction.Toolkit;

public class RaySelectableColorChange : MonoBehaviour
{
    [SerializeField] private Material hoverMaterial;
    [SerializeField] private Material defaultMaterial;
    private MeshRenderer meshRenderer;
    private XRSimpleInteractable interactable;

    void Awake()
    {
        meshRenderer = GetComponent<MeshRenderer>();
        interactable = GetComponent<XRSimpleInteractable>();

        if (interactable != null)
        {
            interactable.firstHoverEntered.AddListener(OnRayHoverEnter);
            interactable.lastHoverExited.AddListener(OnRayHoverExit);
            interactable.selectEntered.AddListener(OnRaySelect);
        }
    }

    private void OnDestroy()
    {
        if (interactable != null)
        {
            interactable.firstHoverEntered.RemoveListener(OnRayHoverEnter);
            interactable.lastHoverExited.RemoveListener(OnRayHoverExit);
            interactable.selectEntered.RemoveListener(OnRaySelect);
        }
    }

    private void OnRayHoverEnter(HoverEnterEventArgs args)
    {
        if (meshRenderer != null && hoverMaterial != null)
        {
            meshRenderer.material = hoverMaterial;
            Debug.Log("Ray Hovered: " + gameObject.name);
        }
    }

    private void OnRayHoverExit(HoverExitEventArgs args)
    {
        if (meshRenderer != null && defaultMaterial != null)
        {
            meshRenderer.material = defaultMaterial;
            Debug.Log("Ray Exited: " + gameObject.name);
        }
    }

    private void OnRaySelect(SelectEnterEventArgs args)
    {
        Debug.Log("Ray Selected: " + gameObject.name + " by " + args.interactorObject.transform.name);
        // Add specific action here, e.g., activate a function
    }
}
Testing Checklist
  • Confirm the controller's XR Ray Interactor and Line Visual are enabled.
  • Point at the cube: hover should swap material and log a hover message.
  • Press trigger: select log should include the interactor name.
Misconception: seeing the line visual does not mean the ray hits the object. Always verify hover events fire before assuming select will work.

screens.title: Gaze vs Pointer — Choosing the Right Input
screens.subtitle: When to prefer gaze selection and when a ray pointer is better

narration.text: Choosing between gaze and pointer depends on context, ergonomics, and precision needs. Gaze is low-friction and great for quick choices or when the user's hands aren't available. A gaze-driven menu where selection occurs after a short dwell is simple and accessible for many mobile VR scenarios. However, gaze struggles with precision when targets are small or when the user’s head is unstable. Pointer interactions provide explicit aiming and are preferable for manipulation, dragging, or when exact placement matters. A controller-based ray allows users to aim at small UI elements or pick up objects at a distance. Compare two concrete examples: a gaze-activated menu for quick scene changes versus a ray pointer used to select and move a remote tool. Misconception: some designers assume gaze avoids the need for feedback, but both input types require clear hover and selection cues. For gaze, showing dwell progress prevents guessing. For pointer interactions, a reticle and hover color confirm intent. In many practical systems, combine both: offer gaze as a primary method on headset-only builds and provide ray pointers when controllers are present. Ask yourself: does the task demand aiming precision? If yes, favor a pointer; if not and hands are unavailable, use gaze with strong feedback.

keyIdea.title: Choosing inputs
keyIdea.text: Use gaze for hands-free, low-precision tasks with dwell feedback; use pointer rays for precision and manipulation. Combine both when appropriate.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Gaze vs Pointer — Choosing the Right Input
Gaze Interaction
Strengths: hands-free, simple to discover. Weaknesses: poor precision, head jitter sensitivity.
Example: gaze a scene button for 2 seconds to change level.
Design tip: add radial progress and hover color to reduce false activations.
Pointer (Ray) Interaction
Strengths: precise aiming and manipulation. Weaknesses: requires a controller or hand-tracking, can be more complex to tune.
Example: use a controller ray to pick up and move a remote object.
Design tip: ensure Interaction Layer Mask includes the object's layer and show a reticle for hit feedback.

screens.title: Setup Steps: Gaze and Ray Interactors
screens.subtitle: A step-by-step checklist to create the two interactors and ready your scene

narration.text: Follow these steps to set up both gaze and ray interactions in a Unity scene. Step one: add an XR Origin to your scene if you don't already have one. Step two: for gaze, attach an XR Gaze Interactor to the Main Camera or a child representing the head. Step three: add XRSimpleInteractable to any target GameObject, and set Gaze Dwell Time to a non-zero value when you want automatic dwell selection. Step four: for pointer input, attach XR Ray Interactor and XR Interactor Line Visual to the LeftHand and RightHand controller GameObjects under XR Origin. Step five: set the Interaction Layer Mask on each interactor so it includes the layers your interactables sit on. Step six: ensure target objects have non-trigger colliders and, if they need physics, an appropriate Rigidbody. Step seven: attach scripts that subscribe to hover and select events to change visuals or perform actions. As you work, test each step in Play Mode. Verify hover logs before testing selection. If selection fails, re-check the interaction mask, collider type, and whether dwell time is configured. This flow helps you build incrementally and catch configuration errors early.

keyIdea.title: Setup checklist
keyIdea.text: Add XR Gaze Interactor to the camera, add XR Ray Interactor and Line Visual to controllers, set layer masks, add colliders, and attach event scripts.

screens.title: Interaction Components and Events
screens.subtitle: How Interactors, Interactables, Line Visuals, and events fit together

narration.text: Understanding the roles of components makes setup predictable. An Interactor is an input source — either the XR Gaze Interactor or the XR Ray Interactor — that casts a ray and issues hover and select intentions. An Interactable is a target object that exposes events via XRSimpleInteractable, such as firstHoverEntered, lastHoverExited, and selectEntered. The XR Interactor Line Visual decorates an interactor with a visible laser and reticle, but it does not change hit logic. Events travel from the Interactor to the Interactable: when the interactor's ray hits the collider, the interactable raises hover events that your scripts can subscribe to. Scripts attached to the interactable are responsible for swapping materials, playing sounds, or executing gameplay logic. A typical architecture: XR Origin contains Camera and Controller GameObjects; camera hosts XR Gaze Interactor, controllers host XR Ray Interactors and Line Visuals; scene objects host XRSimpleInteractable, Collider, optional Rigidbody, and a script that responds to events. Misconception: adding an Interactor alone does little; you must add XRSimpleInteractable to scene objects and ensure layer masks align. Keep this component map in mind when diagnosing missed interactions.

keyIdea.title: Component roles
keyIdea.text: Interactors emit intent, Interactables expose events; Line Visuals present the ray visually. Scripts subscribe to interactable events to enact feedback or behavior.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Interaction Components and Events
Component Map
XR Origin • Camera (XR Gaze Interactor) • Left/Right Hand (XR Ray Interactor + Line Visual)
Interactable Node
XRSimpleInteractable + Collider (+ Rigidbody if physics-driven) + script subscribing to hover/select events.
Event Flow
  1. Interactor casts ray.
  2. Ray hits Collider on an Interactable.
  3. Interactable fires firstHoverEntered; scripts can respond.
  4. On input or dwell completion, selectEntered fires.
Tip: the XR Interactor Line Visual only draws visuals. Event routing depends on masks, colliders, and the interactable component.

screens.title: Troubleshooting Raycast and Collider Issues
screens.subtitle: Diagnose why a ray might pass through an object and how to fix it

narration.text: When a controller ray fails to interact with an object that has XRSimpleInteractable and a Collider, follow a tight troubleshooting process. First, confirm the object’s layer is included in the interactor's Interaction Layer Mask — mismatch here is the most frequent cause of missed hits. Second, check the Collider: ensure it is enabled, appropriately sized, and not unintentionally set as a trigger unless you have a Rigidbody configured for trigger detection. Third, inspect Rigidbodies: a trigger collider without a Rigidbody sometimes prevents expected ray behavior in certain physics setups; adding a kinematic Rigidbody can help. Fourth, test visibility: use simple geometry and a visible material and confirm the line visual and reticle indicate a hit on other objects. Fifth, look at event logs: add Debug. Log calls in your hover and select callbacks to verify whether events are firing but visuals are not updating. A common misdiagnosis is assuming code is wrong when the layer mask is incorrect. Always test with a minimal cube, minimal script that logs hover events, and a default interaction mask. These steps narrow the cause quickly and keep fixes straightforward.

keyIdea.title: Troubleshooting checklist
keyIdea.text: Check Interaction Layer Mask, collider enabled/trigger state, Rigidbody configuration, and verify hover events via logs before changing scripts.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Troubleshooting Raycast and Collider Issues
Quick Checks
  • Interaction Layer Mask includes object layer.
  • Collider enabled and sized correctly.
  • Trigger colliders paired with Rigidbody if needed.
Logging & Isolation
Attach a minimal script that logs firstHoverEntered and selectEntered. Use a minimal test scene with one cube to isolate the issue from complex scene hierarchies.
If logs never show hover, the problem is likely a mask or collider. If hover logs fire but visuals don't update, check your material handling and renderer references.
Fix Example
If ray passes through: open the controller's XR Ray Interactor, confirm Interaction Layer Mask contains the object's layer, then toggle the collider's enabled state to refresh physics. Add Debug.Log statements to trace event firing.

screens.title: Activity Walkthrough: Build and Test Two Cubes
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step live-coding lab to create a gaze cube and a ray cube and validate interaction

narration.text: This hands-on activity brings the previous lessons into a short live-coding workflow you can follow. Start with an empty scene that contains an XR Origin. Create two cubes and position them in front of the origin: one at (0, 1, 3) for gaze, another at (2, 1, 5) for ray testing. Create two materials: HoverMaterial (bright green) and DefaultMaterial (grey). Assign DefaultMaterial to both cubes. For the gaze cube, add XRSimpleInteractable and set Gaze Dwell Time to two seconds. Create and attach the GazeInteractableColorChange script, and assign the material fields in the Inspector. Ensure the Main Camera has XR Gaze Interactor. For the ray cube, add XRSimpleInteractable, attach RaySelectableColorChange script, and assign materials. Add XR Ray Interactor and XR Interactor Line Visual to both controller GameObjects under XR Origin. Set their Interaction Layer Masks to include the cubes' layer. Enter Play Mode, look at the first cube for two seconds to validate color change and selection logs, then use the controller ray to hover over the second cube, watch the hover color change, and press the trigger to see the selection log. If something fails, use the troubleshooting checklist: layer masks, colliders, and rigidbody setup.

keyIdea.title: Lab walkthrough
keyIdea.text: Create two cubes, add XRSimpleInteractable and the provided scripts, set dwell and line visuals, then test hover and select flows in Play Mode.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Activity Walkthrough: Build and Test Two Cubes
Scene Setup
  1. Create XR Origin and two cubes at (0,1,3) and (2,1,5).
  2. Create HoverMaterial and DefaultMaterial; assign Default to both cubes.
  3. Add XRSimpleInteractable to each cube.
Scripts and Components
  1. Attach GazeInteractableColorChange to the gaze cube; set Gaze Dwell Time = 2s; ensure Main Camera has XR Gaze Interactor.
  2. Attach RaySelectableColorChange to the ray cube; add XR Ray Interactor and XR Interactor Line Visual to controllers.
  3. Set Interaction Layer Masks to include cube layer.
Test & Validate
Enter Play Mode: gaze at the first cube for two seconds to see color change. Point the controller ray at the second cube to see hover color, then press trigger to see select log. If anything fails, follow the troubleshooting checklist.

First, gaze interaction selects by looking and relies on XR Gaze Interactor and XRSimpleInteractable with dwell timers. Second, pointer interaction uses XR Ray Interactor and XR Interactor Line Visual to allow precise aiming and selection with controller input. Third, Interaction Layer Mask is critical: if layers don’t match, rays will pass through objects. Fourth, visual feedback is essential for both input types: color changes, scale, outlines, or progress indicators give users confidence that their input is recognized. Keep these concepts in mind while building and testing; they will guide choices about which input model to use and how to surface selection state to the user. Gaze Interaction

Pointer Interaction
Use XR Ray Interactor and controllers for precise aiming and selection.
XR Interactor Line Visual
Draws the ray and reticle but does not affect hit logic; it communicates intent to the user.

narration.text: A final compact checklist of technical primitives and UX responsibilities: XR Gaze Interactor attaches to the camera to support gaze; XR Ray Interactor attaches to controllers to support pointing. XRSimpleInteractable is the target component that exposes hover and select events your scripts consume. Interaction Layer Mask filters which objects an interactor can hit and is often the reason rays miss objects. Visual feedback is your responsibility: change materials, scale, or show outlines and progress rings so users understand when they are hovering or when a selection is about to occur. Keep testing with simple cubes to validate each part — interactor, layer mask, collider, events, and feedback — before scaling to full scenes.
